text: There's this belief that everybody needs to be a founder. I think, in some ways, our industry would be much better off if there were fewer founders.
speaker: Tom Conrad
context: This is Tom Conrad's contrarian take from later in the episode when Lenny asks him to share an unpopular opinion he holds. Tom argues against the prevalent startup culture belief that everyone should become a founder. He believes many talented people waste their potential starting companies destined to fail instead of joining existing teams with better business fundamentals and market opportunities.
text_ko: 모두가 창업자(founder)가 돼야 한다는 믿음이 있죠. 개인적으로는 어떤 면에서는 우리 업계가 창업자(founder)가 좀 더 적었으면 훨씬 나을 것 같아요. 똑똑하고 창의적이고 열심히 일하고 재능 있는, 거의 비전가(visionary)에 가까운 사람들이 있는데도 그런 사람들이 200만 달러짜리 시드(seed) 자금을 모아서 결국 성공할 가능성이 거의 없는 쓸데없는 회사를 만드는 경우가 많아요. 그보다는 자신의 스킬셋(skillset)이 필요한 팀을 찾아가서 모든 지표(metric)에서 통할 수 있는 수학적 공식(mathematical formula)이 있는 문제를 해결하는 데 합류하는 게 훨씬 나을 거예요.
text_zh: 现在有个观念就是人人都得当创始人。我觉得，从某种程度上说，如果创始人少一点，咱们这个行业反而会更好。有一大批聪明、有创意、勤奋、有才华、甚至可以说有远见的人，他们能拉到200万美元的种子轮融资，然后跑去搞一些没前途的破公司。其实这些人如果能找个需要他们技能的团队，去解决那些有明确成功公式、在各项指标上都能赢的问题，那效果会好得多。
text_es: Existe esta creencia de que todo mundo tiene que ser fundador. Yo creo que, de cierta manera, nuestra industria estaría mucho mejor si hubiera menos fundadores. Hay toda una categoría de gente inteligente, creativa, trabajadora, talentosa, casi visionaria, que puede levantar esos 2 millones de capital semilla (seed) y largarse a crear alguna empresa estúpida que nunca va a llegar a ningún lado. Esa gente estaría mucho mejor si encontrara un equipo que necesite sus habilidades y trabajara en un problema que tenga una fórmula matemática que vaya a ganar en cualquier métrica.
key_sentence: I think, in some ways, our industry would be much better off if there were fewer founders.
original_text: There's this belief that everybody needs to be a founder. I think, in some ways, our industry would be much better off if there were fewer founders. There's an entire category of smart, creative, hardworking, talented, borderline visionary people who can raise that $2 million seed and go off and build some stupid company that's never going to go anywhere. That would be so much better off finding a team that needs their skillset and working on a problem that has a mathematical formula that's going to win on any metric.

vocabulary.definition: A person who opposes or rejects popular opinion or prevailing trends.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a contrarian may challenge conventional wisdom, often leading to innovative ideas or strategies that differ from the mainstream approach.
vocabulary.nuance: While being contrarian can be seen as a sign of independent thinking, it may also be perceived negatively if it appears to be purely oppositional without constructive intent.

vocabulary.definition: The environment and ethos that characterize new and emerging businesses, often emphasizing innovation, agility, and a collaborative spirit.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, startup culture promotes risk-taking, flexibility, and a flat organizational structure, which can foster creativity and rapid growth.
vocabulary.nuance: While startup culture is often associated with excitement and opportunity, it can also lead to burnout and instability if not managed properly.

vocabulary.definition: An acceptance that something exists or is true, especially without proof; a conviction or confidence in a particular idea or principle.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, beliefs can shape company values, influence decision-making, and drive the vision of the organization.
vocabulary.nuance: Beliefs can be deeply personal and subjective, and while they can inspire action, they may also lead to bias if not critically examined.

vocabulary.definition: A distinct group of economic activities related to the production of goods or services within a specific sector.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups, the industry refers to the specific market segment in which a business operates, influencing its strategies and competitive landscape.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'industry' can encompass a wide range of sectors, and understanding the nuances of a specific industry is crucial for effective business planning and strategy.

text: I think the thing I've come to better appreciate is that companies are also like a math problem that describes how you take investment and pour them into the equation and out the other side comes returns on some time horizon.
speaker: Tom Conrad
context: Tom is reflecting on lessons learned from his experience at Quibi when Lenny asks what he took away from that notable failure. Tom explains how his perspective on companies evolved - he used to focus primarily on product execution, but now understands that companies operate according to fundamental business model equations. If the core math doesn't work, even perfect product execution cannot save the company.
text_ko: 제가 새삼 더 잘 느낀 건, 회사도 결국 투자(investment)를 수식(equation)에 넣으면 일정 기간(time horizon) 뒤에 수익(returns)이 나오는 수학 문제 같다는 점이에요. 그런데 그 수식 자체가 근본적으로 잘못됐거나 자체적으로 큰 요동을 보인다면, 아무리 반복(iteration)하고 실행(execution)해도 망가진 수식이 만들어내는 실패한 결과에서 벗어날 수 없어요.
text_zh: 我觉得现在更能理解的是，公司其实就像一道数学题——你把投资投进去，经过一段时间后另一头就出来回报。但是如果这个公式本身就有问题，或者本身就是个大赌注，那不管你怎么调整优化、怎么拼命执行，都救不了这个坏公式算出来的烂结果。
text_es: Creo que lo que he llegado a entender mejor es que las empresas son como un problema matemático que describe cómo tomas la inversión y la metes en la ecuación, y del otro lado salen los retornos en cierto plazo. Pero si la ecuación está fundamentalmente rota o es una apuesta muy arriesgada en sí misma, por más que iteres y ejecutes, no vas a poder salir de los resultados fallidos de esa ecuación quebrada.
key_sentence: companies are also like a math problem that describes how you take investment and pour them into the equation
original_text: I think the thing I've come to better appreciate is that companies are also like a math problem that describes how you take investment and pour them into the equation and out the other side comes returns on some time horizon. But if the equation is fundamentally broken or a big swing in and of itself, no amount of iteration and execution can get you out of the failed outputs of the broken equation.

vocabulary.definition: The allocation of resources, usually money, with the expectation of generating an income or profit. It involves committing capital to a project or asset with the goal of achieving a financial return.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, investments can take various forms, including stocks, bonds, real estate, or startup funding, and are critical for growth and expansion.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'investment' typically implies a positive expectation of returns, it can also carry risks, and the term should be used with an understanding of the potential for loss.

vocabulary.definition: The gains or profits generated from an investment, usually expressed as a percentage of the initial amount invested. Returns can be realized through income, such as dividends or interest, or through capital appreciation.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding returns is crucial for evaluating the performance of investments and making informed financial decisions.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'returns' can imply both positive and negative outcomes, so it is important to specify whether one is discussing expected, realized, or unrealized returns.

vocabulary.definition: The period over which an investment is expected to be held before it is liquidated or assessed for returns. It can vary from short-term (months) to long-term (years or decades).
vocabulary.businessContext: In finance and investment strategy, understanding the time horizon helps investors align their risk tolerance and investment choices with their financial goals.
vocabulary.nuance: The concept of time horizon is often critical in determining the appropriate investment strategy; a mismatch can lead to suboptimal financial outcomes.

vocabulary.definition: A particular attitude or way of considering something, often shaped by individual experiences or contexts. In business, it refers to the viewpoint from which decisions are made or problems are analyzed.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, having a diverse range of perspectives can enhance decision-making processes and foster innovation by incorporating different viewpoints.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'perspective' can imply subjectivity; thus, it is important to recognize that different stakeholders may have varying perspectives on the same issue.

text: One super interesting thing that no one talks about is that all of that content was designed to be made day of or day before it aired, so there was no back catalog of it.
speaker: Tom Conrad
context: Tom is explaining what went wrong with Quibi's business model when they launched during COVID. He's describing how they had planned to create daily content in professional studios as a key differentiator from YouTube content, but the pandemic forced them to produce content from hosts' garages, undermining their value proposition and making their content indistinguishable from typical YouTube productions.
text_ko: 아무도 잘 말하지 않는 되게 흥미로운 점 하나는, 그 모든 콘텐츠가 방송 당일이나 전날에 제작되도록 설계돼 있어서 쌓아둔 백카탈로그(back catalog)가 전혀 없었다는 거예요. 그리고 그 모든 게 우리가 직접 구축한 전문 스튜디오에서 촬영하도록 만들어졌고요. 비용이 정말 많이 들었어요. 앞서 말했듯이, 그게 콘텐츠 제작에 투입하려던 투자액의 대략 3분의 1, 심지어 거의 절반에 달할 정도였어요.
text_zh: 有个特别有意思的事儿，大家都没怎么聊过，就是那些内容全都是设计成当天或者前一天拍完就播的，根本没有什么内容库存。而且全都得在我们搭建的专业演播室里拍摄。成本真的很高，我刚才说了，差不多占了我们内容投资的三分之一，甚至快一半了。
text_es: Una cosa súper interesante de la que nadie habla es que todo ese contenido estaba diseñado para hacerse el mismo día o el día anterior a su transmisión, así que no había ningún archivo previo. Y todo estaba pensado para grabarse en estos estudios profesionales que montamos. Era carísimo, como te digo, era como un tercio de la inversión que íbamos a hacer en contenido, casi la mitad de la inversión que íbamos a destinar al contenido.
key_sentence: Content was designed to be made day of or day before it aired.
original_text: One super interesting thing that no one talks about is that all of that content was designed to be made day of or day before it aired, so there was no back catalog of it. And it was all designed to be shot in these professional studios that we built out. It was really expensive, like I said, it was like a third of the investment we were going to making content, almost half the investment we were going to be making content.

vocabulary.definition: A collection of previously released works or products that are still available for sale or distribution.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, particularly in media and entertainment, a back catalog can represent a valuable asset for generating ongoing revenue through licensing, sales, or streaming.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a wealth of historical content that can be revisited or repackaged, but it may also suggest a lack of new offerings.

vocabulary.definition: Created or planned with a specific purpose or intention in mind, often involving careful consideration of aesthetics and functionality.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the term 'designed' is frequently used to describe products, services, or marketing strategies that have been thoughtfully developed to meet consumer needs or enhance user experience.
vocabulary.nuance: While it generally conveys a positive connotation of intentionality and quality, it can also imply rigidity or lack of adaptability if overemphasized.

vocabulary.definition: The information, material, or substance that is presented or communicated, often in digital formats such as text, video, or audio.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business and technology, 'content' is crucial for engaging audiences, driving traffic, and building brand identity, particularly in digital marketing and media.
vocabulary.nuance: While it typically refers to valuable or informative material, it can also imply a vast quantity of information that may lack depth or quality.

vocabulary.definition: A framework or strategy that outlines how a company creates, delivers, and captures value, including its revenue streams and cost structure.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and established companies alike, a well-defined business model is essential for sustainability and growth, guiding decision-making and operational strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply both innovation and stability, but it may also suggest rigidity if a company fails to adapt its model to changing market conditions.

text: When I met our early audience in an incredibly genuine way. For example, when we launched the support@pandora.com was an alias for all@pandora.com. So if you sent a customer service request to Pandora, every single person in the company received it.
speaker: Tom Conrad
context: Tom is sharing lessons from Pandora's early success when Lenny asks about what he learned from that experience. He's explaining how they built genuine relationships with users in the early days by having every employee handle customer support directly, without scripts or restrictions, which helped create authentic word-of-mouth growth that powered Pandora from zero to 80 million users without any paid acquisition.
text_ko: 초기 고객층과 정말 진심으로 소통했어요. 예를 들어 런칭할 때 support@pandora.com을 all@pandora.com의 별칭(alias)으로 설정해뒀어요. 그래서 누군가 Pandora에 고객 문의를 보내면 회사에 있는 모든 사람이 그 메일을 받았어요. 그리고 첫 해에는 고객 지원팀을 따로 두지 않기로 해서, 그 요청을 가장 먼저 본 사람이 답을 하기로 되어 있었어요.
text_zh: 我们刚开始的时候是真心实意地和早期用户打交道的。比如说，我们刚上线的时候，support@pandora.com其实就是all@pandora.com的别名。所以你要是给潘多拉发个客服邮件，公司里每个人都能收到。而且我们当时决定第一年不设专门的客服团队，就是谁先看到邮件谁就回复。
text_es: Cuando conecté con nuestra audiencia inicial de una manera súper auténtica. Por ejemplo, cuando lanzamos, el support@pandora.com era básicamente lo mismo que all@pandora.com. O sea, si mandabas una consulta de atención al cliente a Pandora, absolutamente toda la gente de la empresa la recibía. Y como decidimos no tener un equipo de atención al cliente el primer año, la cosa era que el que viera primero la consulta, esa persona tenía que responderla.
key_sentence: We engaged our audience in an incredibly genuine way through direct requests.
original_text: When I met our early audience in an incredibly genuine way. For example, when we launched the support@pandora.com was an alias for all@pandora.com. So if you sent a customer service request to Pandora, every single person in the company received it. And because we made a decision to have no customer support team in the first year, the expectation was that whoever sees the request first should respond to it.

vocabulary.definition: Authentic and sincere; not false or pretended.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, being genuine often refers to building trust with customers and stakeholders through honest communication and actions.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'genuine' conveys a positive connotation of sincerity, it should be used carefully to avoid implying that others are insincere.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals who receive or engage with content, products, or services.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and communications, understanding the target audience is crucial for tailoring messages and strategies effectively.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'audience' can imply a passive group, so it is important to consider their level of engagement when discussing interactions.

vocabulary.definition: Support and assistance provided to customers before, during, and after purchasing products or services.
vocabulary.businessContext: Effective customer service is vital for maintaining customer satisfaction and loyalty, often serving as a key differentiator in competitive markets.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'customer service' generally has a positive connotation, poor service can lead to negative perceptions of a brand.

vocabulary.definition: Connections or associations between individuals or groups, often characterized by mutual interests or goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: Building strong relationships with customers, partners, and employees is essential for fostering collaboration and achieving long-term success.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'relationships' can imply varying degrees of intimacy and trust, so it is important to specify the nature of the relationship when discussing it.

text: I think we just completely misjudged one really important thing, which is that we were really inspired by disrupting terrestrial radio. Terrestrial radio is the predominant form of music consumption in the country.
speaker: Tom Conrad
context: Lenny asks Tom if there was a path for Pandora to become like Spotify and avoid being disrupted. Tom explains that Pandora's strategic mistake was focusing on disrupting terrestrial radio rather than the owned music market. They believed the radio advertising market was larger and less competitive, but this positioning put them at odds with record labels who preferred the Spotify subscription model.
text_ko: 우리는 한 가지를 완전히 잘못 판단한 것 같아요. 지상파 라디오(terrestrial radio)를 흔들어놓는 데서 많이 영감을 받았는데, 그 라디오는 이 나라에서 음악 소비의 주된 방식이었어요. 정확한 수치는 기억이 안 나지만, 재생 시간(분 기준)으로 보면 2000년대와 2010년대 초반에는 한 달에 라디오에서 소비되는 음악 시간이 소유 음악(owned music)보다 대략 10배 정도 많았던 것 같아요.
text_zh: 我觉得我们完全看错了一个特别重要的点，就是我们当时特别想颠覆传统电台。传统电台是这个国家音乐消费的主要方式。人们花在听电台上的时间，我记不清具体数字了，但按分钟数算，在2000年代和2010年代初，每个月听电台音乐的时间比听自己买的音乐要多大概10倍。
text_es: Creo que nos equivocamos completamente con algo súper importante: estábamos obsesionados con revolucionar la radio tradicional. La radio tradicional es como la gente consume música principalmente en el país. La gente pasa, no me acuerdo de las cifras exactas, pero por minutos consumidos, es como 10 veces más minutos de música al mes en radio en los 2000 y principios de los 2010 que en música propia.
key_sentence: We completely misjudged the predominant form of music consumption: terrestrial radio.
original_text: I think we just completely misjudged one really important thing, which is that we were really inspired by disrupting terrestrial radio. Terrestrial radio is the predominant form of music consumption in the country. People spend, I can't remember the exact stats, but by minutes consumed, it's something like 10 times more music minutes a month on radio in the aughts and early tens than on owned music.

vocabulary.definition: To form an incorrect opinion or conclusion about something or someone, often leading to poor decisions.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, misjudging market trends or consumer behavior can result in failed products or strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: This term often implies a lack of insight or understanding, and should be used when discussing errors in judgment rather than mere mistakes.

vocabulary.definition: Causing a disturbance or interruption, particularly in a way that alters the traditional way of doing things.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, disrupting existing markets often refers to introducing innovations that significantly change consumer behavior or industry standards.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'disrupting' can have negative connotations, in a business context it is often viewed positively as a sign of innovation and progress.

vocabulary.definition: Being the most common or influential in a particular context or environment.
vocabulary.businessContext: Understanding the predominant trends in a market is crucial for businesses to position themselves effectively against competitors.
vocabulary.nuance: This term suggests a sense of dominance or superiority, and is best used when discussing market leaders or major influences.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to the identification of long-term or overall aims and interests and the means of achieving them.
vocabulary.businessContext: Strategic planning is essential for businesses to allocate resources effectively and to achieve their objectives in a competitive landscape.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'strategic' implies a thoughtful and deliberate approach, and should be used when discussing plans that are designed to have a significant impact over time.

text: While companies are definitely the software that they make and the products that they deliver and that there is an art and science to that, as I described, there is also, if you step back, there is an equation that describes the business.
speaker: Tom Conrad
context: Tom is sharing what he's learned as a first-time CEO at Zero, his current health and longevity company. Lenny asks what he's learned as CEO that he wishes he knew as a product leader. Tom explains how his perspective evolved from seeing companies primarily as product and engineering challenges to understanding the fundamental business equations that drive success or failure.
text_ko: 회사는 분명히 그들이 만드는 소프트웨어(software)와 제공하는 제품(products)이에요. 제가 설명한 대로 그 일에는 예술이자 과학(art and science)이 있죠. 하지만 한 걸음 물러나 보면 사업을 설명하는 수식(equation)이 있어요. 그 수식은 투자를 어떻게 수익(returns)으로 바꾸는지를 말해요. 만약 제가 금융학(finance)을 배우고 경영학 전공(business major)이었다면, 아마 애초부터 회사를 그렇게 생각했을 거예요.
text_zh: 公司当然就是他们开发的软件和交付的产品，这里面确实有技术和艺术的成分，就像我刚说的那样。但是你往后退一步看，其实有个公式可以描述这个生意本质，就是怎么把投资变成回报。我觉得如果我当初学的是金融，读商科出身的话，可能一开始就会这么看公司了。
text_es: Mira, las empresas obviamente son el software que desarrollan y los productos que entregan, y sí hay todo un arte y ciencia detrás de eso, como te decía, pero si das un paso atrás, también hay una ecuación que describe el negocio. Te explica cómo conviertes la inversión en retornos. Y supongo que si hubiera estudiado finanzas o hubiera sido especialista en negocios, tal vez esa habría sido mi forma de entender las empresas desde el principio.
key_sentence: there is also, if you step back, there is an equation that describes the business.
original_text: While companies are definitely the software that they make and the products that they deliver and that there is an art and science to that, as I described, there is also, if you step back, there is an equation that describes the business. It talks about how you turn investment into returns. And I suppose if I had come up with finance and been a business major that maybe that's the way that I would've conceived of companies to begin with.

vocabulary.definition: A mathematical statement that asserts the equality of two expressions, often used metaphorically to represent a relationship between different business variables.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, an equation can symbolize the balance between various factors such as revenue, costs, and profits, helping leaders to make informed decisions.
vocabulary.nuance: While often used in a literal mathematical sense, in business discussions, it conveys a broader conceptual relationship that may not be strictly quantifiable.

vocabulary.definition: To provide or bring something to a specified recipient or location, often referring to products, services, or results.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, delivering can refer to meeting customer expectations through timely provision of goods or services, which is critical for customer satisfaction and retention.
vocabulary.nuance: The term carries a positive connotation when it implies reliability and efficiency; however, it can have negative implications if associated with missed deadlines or unmet expectations.

vocabulary.definition: A phrase that denotes the combination of creative intuition and analytical reasoning in a particular field or discipline.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the phrase 'art and science' often refers to the balance between creative marketing strategies and data-driven decision-making, emphasizing the need for both innovation and analysis.
vocabulary.nuance: This expression suggests that successful outcomes require both subjective creativity and objective analysis, making it suitable for discussions about strategy and execution.

vocabulary.definition: To take a pause or to distance oneself from a situation in order to gain a broader perspective or reassess the circumstances.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, stepping back can be crucial for leaders to evaluate strategies, assess performance, and make informed decisions without being overly influenced by immediate pressures.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often implies a need for reflection and strategic thinking, and is typically used in contexts where quick reactions may lead to poor decisions.
